A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the compartmentalization and activity of these two proteins is determined by their structures and by the genetic asymmetry of the chromosome, but that their abundance in each partner cell is determined primarily by the time at which their expression commences.
the partitioning of SpoIIE and σE between the compartments is determined by the combined effects of gene position, protein structure and the timing of protein synthesis.

compartmentalization is achieved by a combination of genetic asymmetry and protein structure, and is not simply the result of a passive sorting of proteins by the asymmetric distribution of the chromosome during sporulation.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the compartmentalization and degradation of σE and of SpoIIE are both influenced by the position of their encoding genes on the chromosome, but that the protein structures of σE and the C terminus of SpoIIE contribute to the efficiency of the compartmentalization process.

compartmentalization of regulatory factors in sporulation can be achieved in a variety of ways, including the use of genetic asymmetry to control the time of entry into the developing compartment of the gene encoding the regulatory factor, the structure of the protein itself and the activity of the protein's cognate partner in the compartment where it would be inappropriate.

the compartmentalization that is a hallmark of endospore formation is not simply a passive consequence of the genetic asymmetry of the sporulating cell, but is actively maintained by the degradation of proteins that have entered the wrong compartment.
